sentences.text: The average adult Daspletosaurus measured 8.5 to 9 meters in length and weighed 2 to 3 metric tons.
However, one large specimen suggests the animal could reach lengths over 9 meters and weights of 4 to 5 metric tons.
It possessed a massive skull reaching more than 1 meter in length.
The type specimen was discovered in 1921 near Steveville, Alberta, by Charles Mortram Sternberg and fully described by Dale Russell in 1970.
Known fossils were recovered from the Oldman Formation, and a paratype was collected by Barnum Brown in 1913.
Daspletosaurus possessed small forelimbs typical of tyrannosaurids, which were proportionately longer than those in other genera.
The predator likely hunted large dinosaurs such as the ceratopsid Centrosaurus and the hadrosaur Hypacrosaurus.
A full-grown individual from the Dinosaur Park Formation bears tyrannosaur bite marks on its skull.
The genus was described by Russell in 1970, with Daspletosaurus torosus as the type species.
Three other species have been proposed, and the genus Thanatotheristes has been suggested as a synonym.
Fossils from the Oldman Formation date between about 79.5 and 77 million years ago, while those from the Dinosaur Park Formation date specifically between 75.6 and 75.0 million years ago.
All known fossils date to the middle to late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, between 78 and 74.4 million years ago, in what is now North America.
It is debated whether an immature specimen from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation belongs to Daspletosaurus, as thorough re-examination favored its referral to Albertosaurus sarcophagus.

Researchers debate whether D. wilsoni is an intermediate species evolving through anagenesis between D. torosus and D. horneri, or if it is a junior synonym, noting that new features in specimen CMC VP 15826 weaken the hypothesis that they are distinct.
